basics.name: School and hobby mechanism education: DT Online wiki (UK Design & Technology), NotesandSketches Mechanisms Module (Laszlo Lipot) and Rob Ives paper automata mechanisms (Essential Mechanisms packs and Mechanism explainer pages)
basics.url: DT Online Mechanisms category: https://wiki.dtonline.org/index.php/Category:Mechanisms ; NotesandSketches Mechanisms Module: https://www.notesandsketches.co.uk/Mechanisms_module.html ; Rob Ives mechanism explainers: https://www.robives.com/mechanism/ and Essential Mechanism shop: https://www.robives.com/essentialmech/
basics.resource_type: Mixed: encyclopedia/wiki (DT Online, a MediaWiki site), teaching notes with animations and tests (NotesandSketches, HTML + PDF pages), and paper model library plus short explainer pages (Rob Ives, a shop of downloadable card-model templates with a membership)
basics.cost: DT Online: free (funded by Amazon affiliate links). NotesandSketches: HTML theory pages and PDFs free online; the terms page says Laszlo Lipot stopped trading in September 2016 and, from 1 January 2017, grants free educational use of resources marked 'free of charge' (older pages still show the old prices: GBP 30 single user, GBP 60 school site licence). Rob Ives: explainer pages free; individual Essential Mechanism templates GBP 5 each (GBP 2.50 each on his Substack page), Essential Mechanisms Pack One (12 models) GBP 15, or membership GBP 39 per year (GBP 35 recurring) that unlocks all downloads; a free account tier exists
basics.license: DT Online: text under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 (stated in the footer and the MediaWiki rights info), so it can be reused with credit for non-commercial purposes if shared alike; linking is always fine. NotesandSketches: all notes, illustrations, animations and PDFs are the copyright of Laszlo Lipot; free use for learning and teaching only, no resale; not an open licence, so link rather than copy. Rob Ives: '(c) Rob Ives 2025' footer, all rights reserved; paid templates are for making your own models, and the membership page says the files are 'fully editable' for your own designs; no reuse licence for images was found, so link only [uncertain]
basics.year: DT Online: builds on the 1980s Acorn 'Design Processor' idea; the current wiki's first upload log entry is 16 October 2014, most mechanism pages last edited 2016-2017 (Mechanisms category page 13 July 2017), and the wiki's latest recent change seen was 24 February 2025 (MediaWiki 1.43.9). NotesandSketches: Flash-era site (late 2000s) [uncertain]; licence change notice dated 2016-2017. Rob Ives: mechanism explainer pages dated 30 September 2010; book 'Paper Automata' (Tarquin) dated 9 July 1998 on his site; 'Making Paper Automata' (Crowood, ISBN 978-0719844874) page dated 4 February 2025; Essential Mechanisms Substack post 30 March 2023; shop items still being added in 2025 (e.g. 'Worm Gear (2025)')
basics.access_barrier: DT Online: none. NotesandSketches: none for the HTML/PDF notes, but the animations are Flash (.swf) files that modern browsers cannot play, so only screenshots show. Rob Ives: none for the explainer pages; paywall (per-item purchase or membership) for the printable templates
basics.image_license: DT Online: mixed; many images are the site's own (CC BY-NC-SA along with the text) but pages also reuse Wikimedia Commons files (e.g. 'Pin tumbler with key.svg') and embed YouTube animations from Nguyen Duc Thang's channel and Thingiverse/Hackaday GIFs, which keep their own licences [uncertain]. NotesandSketches: illustrations and Flash animations copyright Laszlo Lipot, educational use only. Rob Ives: photos and templates all rights reserved
basics.authority_level: educator (DT Online is written by D&T teachers and educationalists; NotesandSketches by a former head of D&T and Brunel University part-time lecturer; Rob Ives is a former teacher and professional paper engineer and author). None is peer-reviewed

coverage.covers: School-level simple machines and mechanisms. DT Online: a Mechanisms category with 5 subcategories (Cams 7 pages, Gears 8, Levers 5, Linkages 5, Pulleys 10) and 19 direct pages (e.g. Ratchet, Crank and Slider, Whitworth Quick Return, Types of Motion, Velocity Ratio, Mechanical Advantage, links to 507 Mechanical Movements and 2100 Animated Mechanical Mechanisms), plus related categories: Fixings and Fastenings (10 pages incl. Hinges and Stays; Locks, Bolts and Catches; Knock Down Fittings; Pins and Clips; Keys, Keyways and Splines), Wood Joints (14 joints), Adhesives (4 pages) and Pneumatics. About 55 mechanism pages plus about 30 joining pages. NotesandSketches: about 30 topic pages (cams and followers, chain and sprocket, couplings incl. flanged, split, flexible and universal joint, crank and slider, bearings of 7 kinds, brakes, clamps, knurling, gears incl. worm and bevel, levers, linkages, pulleys and belts, ratchet and pawl, 5 spring types, screws, ball and roller screws) with 2 x 100-question tests and product-analysis exercises. Rob Ives: 15 short mechanism explainer pages (cam, cams, crank, crank slider, bell crank, piston, levers, linkages, gears, bevel gear, worm gear, rack and pinion, ratchet, Geneva, quick return) and about 55 buildable paper Essential Mechanism models (cams, cranks, gears, Geneva, Scotch yoke, springs, compound mechanisms)
coverage.organisation: DT Online: MediaWiki category tree by D&T curriculum topic (Mechanisms > Cams / Gears / Levers / Linkages / Pulleys), with alphabetical page lists, search, a glossary category and 'Buyers Guides'. Easy for beginners because the topics follow the school syllabus and use everyday examples (scissors, bicycles, door handles). NotesandSketches: a single module index page grouped by topic (motion, levers, linkages, cams, gears, pulleys, friction, bearings, springs, screws), then exercises. Rob Ives: a paged list of mechanism explainers and a shop category of models; the Essential Mechanisms pack groups 12 models into 4 families (Cams, Cranks, Gears, Compound). All three start from 'what kind of motion do you want' (rotary, linear, reciprocating, oscillating), which suits beginners
coverage.scope_match: low to medium: they explain the classic school mechanism types (ratchet, cams, crank-slider, Geneva, quick return, worm and bevel gears, linkages) in very plain language, and DT Online also covers adhesive types, knock-down fittings, catches, magnetic gears and solenoids, but the depth is shallow and there is nothing on torque limiters, compliant or print-in-place joints, snap fits or powered latches beyond a basic solenoid page
coverage.taxonomy_used: UK D&T curriculum scheme: four types of motion (linear, rotary, reciprocating, oscillating) plus mechanism families. DT Online: 5 mechanism subcategories (Cams, Gears, Levers, Linkages, Pulleys) under Mechanisms, with separate Fixings and Fastenings, Wood Joints, Adhesives and Pneumatics categories. NotesandSketches: about 13 topic groups (mechanical systems, cams, chain and sprocket, couplings, cranks, friction and bearings, gears, levers, linkages, moments, motion, pulleys and belts, ratchet, springs, screws/motion control). Rob Ives: 4 families in the Essential Mechanisms pack (Cams, Cranks, Gears, Compound Mechanisms)
coverage.example_types: ratchet and pawl (one-way mechanism), linear ratchet (as in cable ties and quick-release bar clamps), Geneva drive / Geneva stop (intermittent motion), double Geneva drive, Whitworth quick-return mechanism, crank and slider, Scotch yoke, bell crank, reverse-motion linkage, parallel-motion linkage, push-pull linkage, four-bar chain, snail cam (drop cam), swashplate, cylindrical (barrel) cam, eccentric cam, worm gear, bevel gear, rack and pinion, idler gear, magnetic gears (slip when overloaded), co-axial counter-rotating drive, fusee, cone pulley, block and tackle, windlass, knock-down (KD) fittings, keys, keyways and splines, flexible and universal-joint couplings, ball screw and roller screw, paper compression spring
coverage.making_methods: School workshop making: card and paper modelling (Rob Ives; DT Online Primary pages), stripwood, MDF and plastic sheet, woodwork joints, simple electronics and pneumatics kits. General design and technology rather than 3D printing, CNC or robotics
coverage.item_count: DT Online: about 55 mechanism pages (19 in Mechanisms plus 35 in its 5 subcategories) and 22 files in the category; whole wiki 576 articles and 2,074 images. NotesandSketches: about 30 mechanism topic pages, 200 test questions and about 15 exercises. Rob Ives: 15 mechanism explainer pages and 56 Essential Mechanism products (40 on page 1 including the pack, 16 on page 2)
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: One-way/ratchet: yes, in all three (DT Online Ratchet page also covers linear ratchets, cable ties and quick-release vice mechanisms; NotesandSketches ratchet and pawl; Rob Ives ratchet explainer and 'Ratchet Mech' model). Indexing/detent: Geneva drive/stop (Rob Ives explainer and Geneva Crank, Double Geneva Drive and 'Index Mechanism' models); no ball-detent page. Gear trains/gearboxes: yes at school level (simple and compound gear trains, idler gears, velocity ratio, worm, bevel, rack and pinion; Rob Ives Two Stage Gear, Gear Box 2:1 and 3:1). Torque-limiting: only indirectly, as DT Online's note that magnetic gears slip when overloaded. Powered connectors: a basic DT Online Solenoid page (mentions electric door locks) and electronic locks in 'Locks, Bolts and Catches'; nothing on electromagnets as latches or motorised locks. Adhesive types: yes, DT Online Adhesive Types (epoxy, contact/impact adhesive, balsa cement, cyanoacrylate, latex/Copydex), Glues and Pastes (PVA), Hot Melt Glues and Adhesive Tapes, with material advice (non-porous plastics, metals, fabrics). Over-centre: not found (toggle clamps not covered) [uncertain]. Self-locking, hand-release only, compliant, print-in-place: not covered
coverage.entry_structure: DT Online: image, Description, Features and Applications, embedded YouTube animations (often Nguyen Duc Thang clips) with one-line captions, Wikipedia links, buyers-guide template, category links. NotesandSketches: a screenshot linking to a Flash animation, a few paragraphs of plain explanation with bold key words, and a printable PDF version. Rob Ives explainers: one small image and 1-2 paragraphs. Rob Ives models: photo, description of the motion ('turn the handle and ...'), video, downloadable PDF template with build instructions
coverage.audience_level: school (UK Key Stages 2-4, ages about 7-16) and hobbyist (paper automata makers, all ages)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: high: all three use short, everyday-language explanations with product examples (winches, fishing reels, bicycles, door handles, cable ties) and introduce the proper term in bold; Rob Ives describes each mechanism by what happens when you turn the handle, and his paper models let a beginner build and hold the mechanism
usefulness.has_images: yes: DT Online has simple labelled diagrams and photos (small, often low-resolution, some GIFs); NotesandSketches has clear textbook-style colour illustrations and animation screenshots; Rob Ives has good product photos of finished paper models and small diagrams on explainer pages
usefulness.has_animations: yes, with caveats: DT Online embeds YouTube animations (mostly from Nguyen Duc Thang's 2100 Animated Mechanical Mechanisms) and a few GIFs (animated radial cam, snail cam, Whitworth quick return, magnetic gears); NotesandSketches animations are Adobe Flash (.swf), which no longer play in current browsers; Rob Ives has YouTube videos of models working
usefulness.gaps: Shallow, school-syllabus coverage: no torque limiters, slip clutches, over-centre latches, cam cleats, bayonet mounts, snap fits, living hinges, compliant or print-in-place joints, harmonic or cycloidal drives; no design numbers for 3D printing; NotesandSketches animations are dead Flash; Rob Ives' buildable content is paywalled and paper-only; DT Online pages are small and some are stale (most edits 2016-2017) with broken-file-link pages
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: yes for DT Online and NotesandSketches, which have stable readable per-topic URLs, e.g. https://wiki.dtonline.org/index.php/Category:Mechanisms and https://www.notesandsketches.co.uk/Ratchet.html (with a PDF at https://www.notesandsketches.co.uk/PDF/Ratchet_and_pawl.pdf); Rob Ives explainer pages are stable too (e.g. https://www.robives.com/mechanism/ratchet/) and product pages suit a 'build a paper model of it' link (e.g. https://www.robives.com/project/essential-mechanisms-pack-one/)
usefulness.reusable_data: DT Online: structured and exportable through the MediaWiki API (https://wiki.dtonline.org/api.php returns category members, page wikitext and revision dates as JSON); reuse of the list and text is allowed under CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (non-commercial, share-alike, attribution). NotesandSketches: scrape-only, copyright, educational use only. Rob Ives: scrape-only shop listings, all rights reserved
usefulness.maintained: DT Online: online, MediaWiki updated to 1.43.9, but mechanism content is largely unchanged since 2016-2017 and only one active user (latest recent change seen 24 February 2025). NotesandSketches: online but frozen since the 2016 trading stop; Flash animations no longer usable. Rob Ives: actively maintained (new models and 2025 book page; footer 2025). Wayback Machine could not be checked from this environment
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Start the flow chart with the four types of motion (linear, rotary, reciprocating, oscillating) using arrow icons, as DT Online and NotesandSketches do. (2) Describe every mechanism by 'turn this and that happens' (Rob Ives) before naming it. (3) Tie each type to everyday products (cable tie = linear ratchet, fishing reel = ratchet and pawl, film projector = Geneva) and to product-analysis exercises. (4) Offer a printable PDF version of each entry (NotesandSketches). (5) Link 'build a cheap cardboard model' options for hands-on learning (Rob Ives Essential Mechanisms). (6) Short self-tests or quizzes per family. (7) DT Online's Adhesive Types page is a compact model for a material-to-glue chooser
usefulness.design_rules_given: Few: school maths only (velocity ratio and gear ratio calculations, mechanical advantage, moments, lever classes); no clearances, fits, strain limits or torque values. DT Online adhesive pages give qualitative advice (contact adhesive left 10 minutes before bonding; acetone softens cyanoacrylate)
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: None; Rob Ives' templates are fixed PDF designs (members get editable files) [uncertain]
usefulness.file_formats: HTML, PDF (NotesandSketches notes and exercises; Rob Ives templates), GIF/PNG/JPG images, Flash SWF (NotesandSketches, obsolete), embedded YouTube video; DT Online also JSON via the MediaWiki API
usefulness.terminology_value: medium: good source for UK school terms and plain aliases (snail cam, bell crank, push-pull linkage, reverse-motion linkage, windlass, knock-down fittings, impact adhesive = contact adhesive, super glue = cyanoacrylate), but not authoritative for engineering naming
usefulness.decision_support: None as a selector; the only guidance is the motion-type grouping, DT Online buyers guides (e.g. Adhesives Buyers Guide) and NotesandSketches problem-solving exercises (choose a mechanism for a pedal bin, door handle, food mixer, waving display). No filters or comparison tables
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: DT Online links to and embeds Nguyen Duc Thang's 2100 Animated Mechanical Mechanisms videos, 507 Mechanical Movements, KMODDL and Wikipedia, so its animations are borrowed rather than original. All three overlap the standard UK D&T mechanisms syllabus (levers, linkages, cams, gears, pulleys) and other school resources such as Technology Student [uncertain]. Rob Ives' mechanisms overlap Cabaret Mechanical Theatre-style automata teaching
